text:
U.K. PM says he will resign as party leader: What happens next?

Burnham asked about his plans after Starmer's resignation

U.K. PM Starmer announces resignation plan

U.K. PM Keir Starmer is resigning: Hear some of his speech from 10 Downing Street

Reform UK scores breakthrough wins in local elections

Just days after winning a byelection that reignited speculation about the Labour Party's future, Andy Burnham arrived at Westminster on Monday to a welcome that felt part celebration, part coronation.

Burnham's path to becoming Britain's next prime minister now appears wide open.

Earlier Monday, Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced he would step down as Labour leader after just two years in office, acknowledging that his party no longer believed he was the right person to lead it into the next election.

The resignation follows months of speculation, poor local election results in May and growing dissatisfaction among Labour MPs.

Burnham, 56, formally confirmed he will seek the leadership. Hours later, former cabinet minister Wes Streeting — widely viewed as the only figure with enough support to mount a serious challenge — endorsed him instead, meaning Burnham could become leader without a contested race.

A former cabinet minister and three-term mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham has built his political identity around what he calls Manchesterism, a platform focused on decentralizing power away from London.

Political analysts say Burnham inherits many of the same challenges that helped bring down Starmer, including sluggish economic growth, strained public services and voter frustration over living costs.

But after a day of rapid developments, Labour appears eager to unite behind a new leader rather than endure another lengthy leadership battle.

Thanks for following our live coverage as it unfolded. You can follow CBCNews.ca for the latest, including this analysis by Chris Brown.

Andy Burnham was formally sworn in as an MP a couple hours ago, following his victory in last week's Makerfield byelection, a result that helped trigger Keir Starmer's decision to step down as prime minister and Labour leader.

Burnham's return to the House of Commons after nearly a decade as mayor of Greater Manchester was met with loud cheers but also jeers from lawmakers as he was sworn in.

One person shouted, "He's not the Messiah!" — a reference to the 1979 Monty Python film Life of Brian, in which the title character is repeatedly mistaken for a religious saviour despite his protests.

Burnham responded that he's "just a naughty boy," finishing the quote from the movie.

Another lawmaker added, "He's not going to turn water to wine!"

After the swearing-in, Burnham posed for selfies and a group photo with dozens of Labour MPs in another part of Parliament.

Britain's next election does not have to be held until 2029. Asked if he would call an early vote if he becomes prime minister, Burnham said: "You're jumping several hurdles ahead there."

-With files from The Associated Press

Starmer's resignation may not have been surprising, but it is still a remarkable moment in British politics, according to former Downing Street policy adviser Patrick Diamond.

Diamond, who headed policy planning at 10 Downing Street from 2000 to 2010, said months of speculation about Starmer's future, poor local election results in May and declining support among both voters and Labour MPs had made his departure seem increasingly inevitable.

Still, Diamond described the resignation as a "shock," even during an unprecedented period of political instability in the U.K.

Diamond said Starmer was seen as saving the Labour Party with his landslide win in 2024. "One would have expected it to survive if not one term, two terms. So for it to really, under Starmer, last only two years is really extraordinary," he told CBC News.

Diamond said Burnham is a seasoned political operator, who spent more than 30 years in politics as an adviser, MP and cabinet minister, but he would inherit many of the same challenges that plagued Starmer.

That includes sluggish economic growth since Britain left the European Union, strained public services and foreign policy pressures.

"The issue that will determine whether his premiership succeeds is the economy," Diamond said, adding that Burnham may eventually have to confront Britain's post-Brexit relationship with the European Union if he hopes to deliver stronger growth.

Downing Street is decidedly calm this afternoon given the political storm that has rumbled through here today.

The famed door of No. 10 Downing Street is bathed in sunshine from the current British heat wave. This door has been a photo op for many Canadian prime ministers standing alongside their British counterparts — but now it's revolving once again. The Starmer era is over and short lived, at almost two years.

After a weekend away from Downing Street, spending it with his family at Chequers — the countryside home of the British PM — Starmer took time to reconsider his future. On Friday he said he would fight any challenger; 72 hours later he stood here in front of a podium announcing  his resignation.

Andy Burnham has barely got his foot in the door of Westminster before it looks like he will be catapulted here to No. 10. His potential rival, former health secretary Wes Streeting, has stepped out of the ring, saying he now supports Burnham.

Labour wants to avoid the political mess that saw long drawn-out leadership contests under the Conservatives' realm. If no one else stands, which is now highly unlikely, the leadership contest is over before it's started. The transition of power will, as Starmer wants, be orderly.

And Larry the resident Downing Street cat, along with the British public, will be once again under a new British prime minister as soon as next month.

People gathered outside 10 Downing Street on Monday expressed a mix of frustration and cautious optimism following Starmer's departure.

Several told CBC News they did not expect a change in leadership to make much difference.

Barry McLean said Burnham would be "basically the same" as Starmer.

"We're from Northern Ireland, it's not gonna make a difference for us. I can't see it making much of a difference to the rest of the world either," he said.

Others said Starmer's exit was not a surprise. Ed Mattinson said a series of controversies had left the government looking increasingly unstable. As a Conservative voter, Mattinson said he was not enthusiastic about the prospect of a Burnham government.

Amanda Corkery said she welcomes Starmer's departure, saying he had not done enough to address economic challenges facing young people. She noted that her university-educated children are carrying significant student debt while struggling to find work and afford housing.

"I never imagined my 25-year-old daughter, going through the education that she did, and being in 20 to 50,000 pounds worth of debt and then being unemployed," Corkery said.

While she said she likes Burnham's energy and leadership style, she questioned whether he would focus on issues affecting Londoners.

Johnny Coleman said voters are more concerned about the cost of living, energy bills and everyday expenses than leadership contests in Westminster.

"Until I see this whole system change, people actually take power and bring down my bills … I'm not taking the whole thing serious. I'm just here to get a few pictures in, that's about it, right?" he said.

-With files from CBC's Sophie Wallace

Prime Minister Mark Carney thanked Starmer for his leadership and friendship in a post on X.

He said it had been a privilege to work alongside Starmer on efforts to support Ukraine, strengthen NATO, improve Arctic co-operation and deepen ties between Canada and the U.K.

"Throughout, and in the face of exceptional challenges, Keir has acted with principle, determination and collaboration," Carney wrote, adding that "the world is safer and allies are more united because of his efforts."

Burnham is seen as being more on Labour’s left than Starmer but his views on most major policies remain somewhat of a mystery.

"The simple truth is we don't know what an Andy Burnham premiership will look like," Jonathan Tonge, a politics professor at the University of Liverpool, told the BBC.

"We know what Greater Manchesterism looks like under Andy Burnham. It's about Andy Burnham spending a lot of the day actually attracting private sector investment into Greater Manchester. Trying to replicate that at a national level is mighty difficult, though."

One major difference between the two politicians may be more of style than substance.

Whereas Starmer has been criticized as being wooden, Burnham is more polished and often speaks without notes.

Still, Harry Quilter-Pinner, executive director at the U.K.-based Institute for Public Policy Research, says that the sense of disillusionment many voters feel is likely too much for any single politician to resolve.

"I think what we are seeing is ... people feeling that the central promise of liberal capitalist societies — which is basically that things will get better, your kids will do better than you do and your wages will go up and your living standards will improve … is fundamentally broken," he told the BBC.Read Chris Brown's full story about how Starmer's support evaporated here.

Burnham spoke a few words to reporters while breathlessly walking along the train platform at Euston station in London.

Burnham said he's "confident in the process" ahead of a Labour leadership contest and that he'll be putting himself forward. He gave brief praise to Starmer for his time in office, as well.

He was asked about a tweet he wrote in 2022 following Liz Truss's resignation as prime minister, calling for a general election. If Burnham wins the Labour leadership — it's unclear if there are other contenders with Wes Streeting already backing him — he will become yet another unelected British prime minister.

"My priority today is being sworn in as mayor — as MP for Makerfield," Burnham said with a little chuckle at his slip-up.

His byelection win ended his near decade-long mayorship of the city in North West England.

"It's been very, kind of, sad for me today to leave Greater Manchester. The people have been brilliant to me over the last few years. I've loved every minute of the role. I hope I leave Manchester in a better place. Thanks very much," Burnham said, walking briskly.

One of the previous residents of 10 Downing Street is already offering Burnham advice on what he should do.

Conservative Boris Johnson took over from Teresa May in the spring of 2019 and won a majority government just before Christmas that year. He lasted just over three years in the job.

Like Keir Starmer, his term was cut short by disgruntled MPs.

Johnson's advice for Burnham?

"The clock is ticking," he said, according to AFP. "Your honeymoon will not last long."

"You may be full of brilliant ideas for levelling up your country and you will have a wonderful agenda. But then, you know, some asteroid will hit you like Covid or something."

The takeaway, says Johnson: "Go fast."

There have been a lot of residents moving in and out of 10 Downing Street over the past decade.

Since 2015, in the waning days of David Cameron's premiership in the United Kingdom and the nascent days of Canada's Justin Trudeau era, there have been six British PMs, while we've only had two.

David Cameron's resignation in 2016 after the Brexit vote kick-started the recent leadership volatility in the U.K., as the country navigated Brexit, the pandemic and a cost-of-living crisis.
